b_rows_sample.statement: Context is formalized beyond a bounded-context name as a 5-tuple C=(S_C semantic vocabulary, V_C validity rules, R_C material distinctions, P_C policies, A_C authority model) -- a DDD bounded context is thus a semantic and governance environment.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \llbracket x\rrbracket_{C_1}\neq\llbracket x\rrbracket_{C_2}. Same representation \not\Rightarrow same meaning.
b_rows_sample.statement: Bounded context as semantic space: an object x has meaning through a context-relative denotation [[x]]_C, and the same representation can have different meanings under different contexts ([[x]]_C1 != [[x]]_C2) -- 'same representation does not imply same meaning' is proposed as a mathematical foundation of DDD bounded contexts.

b_rows_sample.anchor: x_1\sim_\phi x_2\iff\phi(x_1)=\phi(x_2). ... [x]_\phi.
b_rows_sample.statement: Context mapping phi_AB: S_A -> S_B between bounded contexts is not assumed bijective (often partial/many-to-one/one-to-many/conditional/lossy); it induces an equivalence relation x1 ~phi x2 iff phi(x1)=phi(x2) with equivalence classes [x]_phi, giving a rigorous formal handle on information/semantic collapse.

b_rows_sample.anchor: SemanticViolation\iff MaterialDistinction\land UncontrolledCollapse.
b_rows_sample.statement: Semantic loss is formalized precisely: a collapse phi_AB(x1)=phi_AB(x2) where x1 is not~_A x2 is a candidate semantic-loss event, but is an error (SemanticViolation) only if the collapsed distinction belongs to R_A or R_B (i.e. is material) -- SemanticViolation iff MaterialDistinction and UncontrolledCollapse, much stronger than simply 'preserve semantics'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: M_A(x_1,x_2)\land\phi(x_1)=\phi(x_2)\Rightarrow DeclaredLoss
b_rows_sample.statement: Context-specific materiality predicate M_C(x1,x2) ('the distinction between x1 and x2 is material in context C') yields the architectural invariant candidate: M_A(x1,x2) and phi(x1)=phi(x2) implies DeclaredLoss for a transformation crossing from A to B.

b_rows_sample.anchor: T=(K_A,C_A,A_t,P_t,E_t,\tau)\rightarrow(K_B,C_B).
b_rows_sample.statement: Transformation T is progressively enriched from a bare (K_A,C_A)->(K_B,C_B) mapping to a full domain operation T=(K_A,C_A,Actor_t,Policy_t,Evidence_t,tau)->(K_B,C_B), with the DDD distinction Command (expresses intent) -> Transformation (domain operation/process) -> Event (records what happened).

b_rows_sample.anchor: L(K_t)=\{(K_i,T_i,A_i,E_i,\tau_i,C_i)\}. ... KnowledgeOS lineage = typed provenance graph.
b_rows_sample.statement: Lineage is formalized as a typed provenance graph G_L=(V_L,E_L) (nodes=knowledge states/artifacts, edges=transformations carrying metadata (T,A,E,C,tau)), generally a DAG allowing branching (K1->{K2^A,K2^B}) and merging -- substantially stronger than an ordinary version chain.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Auth(a,r,c,p) mean actor a is authorized under role r, context c, and policy p. ... Identity\neq Authority.
b_rows_sample.statement: Authority is formalized as a relation Auth(a,r,c,p) (actor, role, context, policy) rather than A=User; an action is legitimate only if Auth(a,r,c,p)=True, giving Identity != Authority (authenticated but not authorized is possible).

b_rows_sample.anchor: E_q=(source,observation,context,time,method,provenance). ... E_q\xrightarrow{\mathcal I}Q.
b_rows_sample.statement: Evidence is formalized as a 6-tuple E_q=(source,observation,context,time,method,provenance) rather than a boolean Evidence=True, supporting a claim Q via an inferential procedure E_q -I-> Q.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \hat F_n\neq F. Observation\neq PopulationTruth.
b_rows_sample.statement: Statistical interpretation of evidence: the empirical distribution hat F_n(x) estimates but is not identical to the underlying distribution F, giving Observation != PopulationTruth; likewise a confidence interval must never be silently converted into a ProbabilityOfTruth.

b_rows_sample.anchor: P(\theta\mid E)=\frac{P(E\mid\theta)P(\theta)}{P(E)}. ... Bayesian machinery is one possible formalism for representing uncertainty where the domain permits probabilistic interpretation.
b_rows_sample.statement: Bayesian evidence via Bayes' rule is offered as one possible uncertainty formalism, not a mandatory commitment -- must not be introduced merely because 'KnowledgeOS is probabilistic'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Assurance=DeterministicAssurance\cup StatisticalEvidence\cup HumanJudgement.
b_rows_sample.statement: Two assurance modes are distinguished and must not be conflated: Deterministic (I(x)=True/False, e.g. SchemaValid(x)) and Statistical (P(H|E) or an estimator with uncertainty), together with human judgment forming Assurance = DeterministicAssurance union StatisticalEvidence union HumanJudgement; the appropriate mode depends on the invariant.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Hash(x)=h. ... P(X>x). ... Meaning(x,C). ... Authorized(a,p). These require different mathematical structures.
b_rows_sample.statement: Architectural properties are classified by kind, each needing different mathematics: exact (Hash(x)=h), empirical (P(X>x)), interpretive (Meaning(x,C)), normative (Authorized(a,p)) -- resolving the previous risk of treating every architectural property as probabilistically quantifiable.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Set/Logic + Probability/Statistics + Semantics + Graph Theory.
b_rows_sample.statement: KnowledgeOS is proposed to span four mathematical domains: Logic (handles invariants), Statistics (uncertainty and empirical evidence), Semantics (meaning and context), Graph theory (lineage and transformation history) -- a more defensible architecture than reducing everything to one equation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeItem, Transformation, EvidenceRecord, Decision, Policy, ProvenanceRecord. Each aggregate protects its own invariants.
b_rows_sample.statement: Candidate DDD aggregate boundaries (avoiding one enormous transactional aggregate): KnowledgeItem, Transformation, EvidenceRecord, Decision, Policy, ProvenanceRecord, each with its own invariant -- e.g. KnowledgeItem 'cannot change materially without a recorded transition'; Transformation 'cannot be considered governed without an applicable authority/policy decision'; EvidenceRecord 'cannot silently change after being used to support a claim' (a source change must produce a new evidence state); Decision = f(Evidence,Authority,Context,Policy), not authoritative merely by existing; Policy determines AllowedTransformations/RequiredEvidence/RequiredAuthority/RequiredValidation, giving Policy->GovernedTransformation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: ObservationRecorded, EvidenceRegistered, ClaimProposed, KnowledgeAccepted, TransformationRequested, TransformationExecuted, ValidationCompleted, DecisionApproved, KnowledgeSuperseded.
b_rows_sample.statement: Nine candidate domain events forming the temporal history, supporting an event-sourced interpretation K_t = Fold(E_1,...,E_t), i.e. CurrentState = f(EventHistory) -- explicitly noted as an implementation choice, not a mandatory architecture requirement.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \mathcal K=(State,Context,Transformation,Evidence,Authority) with Lineage being generated by the sequence of transformations: L=History(T).
b_rows_sample.statement: The kernel is reduced from the original 6-tuple (K,C,T,A,E,L) to a 5-tuple (K,C,T,E,A) by recognizing Lineage L is not independent but generated by the transformation history: L = History(T) -- an important reduction toward the minimal kernel.

b_rows_sample.anchor: SI=f(K,C,T) ... BP=f(C,T) ... EI=f(K,E) ... GA=f(A,T) ... TL=f(T_{1:n}) ... DA=f(E,T,Policy). ... the seven principles may not be seven fundamental architectural primitives. They may be derived properties.
b_rows_sample.statement: Candidate dependency equations deriving the 6 (of the earlier 7-8) named architectural principles as functions of the minimal kernel: SemanticIntegrity=f(K,C,T), BoundaryPreservation=f(C,T), EpistemicIntegrity=f(K,E), GovernedAction=f(A,T), TemporalLineage=f(T_{1:n}), Assurance/DeterministicAssurance=f(E,T,Policy) -- proposing that these principles may be derived properties rather than independent primitives, precisely the compression the historical audit sought.

group_evidence.why_grouped: labels co-occur in the same contribution's labels[] 3 separate times across the corpus

a_rows_sample.anchor:
The central distinction is: Supported 
eq Accepted 
eq Committed 
eq True. This distinction should become one of the core laws of KnowledgeOS.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the governing distinction of Step 8 as a candidate core law of KnowledgeOS: Supported ≠ Accepted ≠ Committed ≠ True.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The problem ... Strong supporting evidence, No known contradiction, Current, High provenance quality ... Can KnowledgeOS now put P into the Knowledge State as accepted knowledge? Not necessarily. There is a missing concept: AcceptancePolicy. The evidence tells us what the evidence supports. The acce
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues even strong, uncontradicted, current, high-provenance evidence does not automatically warrant acceptance, introducing AcceptancePolicy as the missing concept determining what may be admitted as accepted knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Four epistemic statuses ... Candidate \rightarrow Supported \rightarrow Accepted \rightarrow Committed ... Supported \rightarrow Contested ... Supported \rightarrow Rejected ... Candidate \rightarrow Unresolved ... These are not simply levels of "confidence." They represent different domain states.
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Candidate/Supported/Accepted/Committed as a branching progression (not a confidence scale), with additional branches to Contested, Rejected, and Unresolved, insisting these are distinct domain states.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Candidate ... A proposition becomes a candidate when KnowledgeOS has reason to represent it but does not yet have sufficient basis to accept it. ... LLM extracted from document ... Candidate(P)=True but Accepted(P)=False. This is particularly important for AI-generated knowledge.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Candidate(P) status (proposition represented but not yet accepted), illustrated by an LLM-extracted proposition, flagged as particularly important for AI-generated knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Supported ... Supported_\rho(P) = Assessment_\rho(P)\models SupportCondition_\rho ... The evidence provides a defensible basis for the proposition under the selected assessment policy. But Supported(P)\not\Rightarrow Accepted(P).
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Supported_ρ(P) as Assessment_ρ(P) satisfying a policy-specific SupportCondition_ρ, explicitly not implying Accepted(P).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Accepted ... Accept_\rho(P,EA) \rightarrow AcceptedAssertion subject to the acceptance policy. ... One authoritative current source is sufficient ... Two independent observations ... Accepted_{\rho_1}(P)=True while Accepted_{\rho_2}(P)=False. This is not a mathematical contradiction. It is policy de
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Accept_ρ(P,EA)→AcceptedAssertion as policy-relative, showing the same evidence can be Accepted under one policy (single authoritative source) and not under another (requiring two independent observations) — policy dependence, not contradiction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Commitment ... an organization may accept ... but still not be committed to using that assertion as a basis for an operational decision. "We accept that Nexus is 3.69, but migration approval requires an additional infrastructure verification." Accepted(P)\not\Rightarrow Committed(P). Commitment mean
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Commitment as distinct from Acceptance: Accepted(P) ⇏ Committed(P), illustrated by an organization accepting a fact but still requiring additional verification before migration approval; commitment means willingness to rely on the proposition for a defined purpose/action.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Commitment is purpose-dependent ... Commit_\rho(P,Purpose,Authority) ... Commit(P,migration,ArchitectureBoard) may require more than Commit(P,internal research,Engineer). Commit(P,P_1)\neq Commit(P,P_2). This fits our earlier Ideal State principle: I_t(P_1)\neq I_t(P_2).
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Commit_ρ(P,Purpose,Authority) as purpose-dependent, e.g. migration commitment requiring Architecture Board authority versus lighter requirements for internal research, echoing the earlier purpose-dependence of the Ideal State.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Truth remains outside the state machine ... Accepted(P)\neq True(P) and Committed(P)\neq True(P). KnowledgeOS does not have an oracle for reality. It records what is currently supported, accepted, and/or committed under a defined epistemic and governance regime.
a_rows_sample.statement: States that neither Accepted(P) nor Committed(P) equals True(P): KnowledgeOS has no oracle for reality, only records what is supported/accepted/committed under a defined regime.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Formal acceptance function ... \alpha_\rho: EA\times P\times C \rightarrow \mathcal S_A ... \mathcal S_A=\{Candidate,Supported,Accepted,Rejected,Contested,Unresolved\} ... an assertion can be Supported + Contested. So again, we should be careful about a single enum.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines α_ρ:EA×P×C→S_A over six statuses, warning against treating S_A as a single mutually-exclusive enum since e.g. Supported+Contested can co-occur.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Better: acceptance as a multidimensional status ... \Omega_A=(SupportStatus,AcceptanceStatus,CommitmentStatus,ContestStatus) ... Support: Strong, Acceptance: Accepted, Commitment: Committed, Contest: Active. This looks strange initially, but it accurately represents real organizational knowledge.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines acceptance status as a four-dimensional vector Ω_A=(SupportStatus,AcceptanceStatus,CommitmentStatus,ContestStatus), with a worked example showing Accepted+Committed+Contest:Active as coherent, accurately reflecting real organizational knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Why "Accepted + Contested" is possible ... an architecture board has formally accepted ... another architect disputes ... Accepted(P)=True while Contested(P)=True. This is not logically impossible. ... The proposition is institutionally accepted while still being epistemically contested. This is exa
a_rows_sample.statement: Justifies Accepted+Contested coexisting via an architecture-board example (formally accepted decision still disputed by an architect), establishing that epistemic status and governance status must not be collapsed.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Acceptance policy ... \rho_A = AcceptancePolicy ... Evidence requirements N_{independent}\geq2 ... Source requirements Authority(Source)\geq A_{min} ... Temporal requirements Age(e)\leq T_{max} ... Conflict requirements ActiveConflict(P)=False ... Human approval ... Statistical threshold Pr(P\mid E)
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines AcceptancePolicy ρ_A as specifying six example condition types (independent-evidence count, source authority minimum, evidence-age maximum, no active conflict, human approval, statistical threshold) — explicitly examples of policy, not universal law.

a_rows_sample.anchor: This gives us a clean separation ... Mathematics defines what the evidence assessment means. Policy defines when an assessment is sufficient for acceptance. Governance defines who has authority to commit to that knowledge. Assessment \rightarrow AcceptancePolicy \rightarrow Acceptance \rightarrow Go
a_rows_sample.statement: Draws a three-way separation — mathematics (what assessment means), policy (when acceptance is sufficient), governance (who may commit) — formalized as Assessment→AcceptancePolicy→Acceptance→Governance→Commitment.

a_rows_sample.anchor: DDD interpretation ... a bounded context around Knowledge Commitment. Assertion ... EvidenceAssessment ... AcceptancePolicy ... AcceptanceDecision ... Commitment ... Authority ... These should not be hidden inside the Assertion entity.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a Knowledge Commitment bounded context with six concepts (Assertion, EvidenceAssessment, AcceptancePolicy, AcceptanceDecision, Commitment, Authority) that must not be hidden inside the Assertion entity.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Acceptance is a domain event ... AssertionAccepted should be emitted. AssertionId, AssessmentId, PolicyId, PolicyVersion, Authority, Context, EffectiveFrom, DecisionBasis, Timestamp. This creates an auditable transition.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines an AssertionAccepted domain event carrying AssertionId, AssessmentId, PolicyId/Version, Authority, Context, EffectiveFrom, DecisionBasis, Timestamp for auditability.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Rejection is different from absence of acceptance ... NotAccepted\neq Rejected ... Evidence: insufficient ... The correct state may be Unresolved. It does not mean P=False. Unresolved\neq Rejected. This is critical for incomplete real-world knowledge.
a_rows_sample.statement: States NotAccepted≠Rejected and Unresolved≠Rejected: insufficient evidence should yield Unresolved, not a claim that P is false — critical for incomplete real-world knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Example ... Production Nexus is backed up. ... Infrastructure engineer says yes ... Backup configuration not inspected ... No restore test ... Support: Moderate, Uncertainty: High, Verification: Insufficient ... KnowledgeOS should not conclude \neg P. Nor Accepted(P). The correct result may be Unres
a_rows_sample.statement: Works a backup-verification example where weak/unverified evidence (engineer's verbal yes, uninspected config, no restore test) correctly yields Unresolved(P) with a Lord recommendation to verify configuration and run a restore test, rather than either Accepted(P) or ¬P.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Acceptance and Ideal State ... MustBeVerified(BackupStatus) ... Supported(P) may still fail the ideal requirement: \Sigma_K(P)\not\models I^K(P). Accepted(P) \not\Rightarrow IdealSatisfied(P). A proposition can be accepted while the knowledge objective remains incomplete.
a_rows_sample.statement: Connects Acceptance to the Ideal State: Accepted(P) ⇏ IdealSatisfied(P) — a proposition can be accepted while the underlying knowledge objective (e.g. independent verification) remains incomplete.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Example ... Nexus = 3.69 Accepted. But the Ideal State requires MustBeKnown, MustBeCurrent, MustBeIndependentlyVerified ... Independent verification = no ... Accepted(P)=True but \Delta_t\neq\emptyset. Acceptance does not mean completion.
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked example: an accepted Nexus-version assertion still leaves a nonempty discrepancy Δ_t because independent verification is missing — 'Acceptance does not mean completion.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: When several pieces of evidence support the same proposition, how should KnowledgeOS combine them? We must avoid the very tempting but incorrect rule: more sources \Rightarrow more certainty. That is only true under specific assumptions.
b_rows_sample.statement: Frames Step 25C.2's question, warning against the tempting-but-incorrect rule 'more sources ⇒ more certainty', true only under specific assumptions.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Start with a controlled proposition ... H="Rollback will succeed if executed." P(H)=0.5. This is an experimental prior, not a KnowledgeOS principle. ... Evidence E_1 ... P(E_1\mid H)=0.95 and P(E_1\mid\neg H)=0.10. LR_1=9.5. O(H)=1. O(H\mid E_1)=9.5. P(H\mid E_1)\approx90.5\% under this specific sta
b_rows_sample.statement: Works a fully numerical Bayesian likelihood-ratio calculation (LR1=9.5) yielding P(H|E1)≈90.5% under an explicit experimental prior, explicitly not a KnowledgeOS principle.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Important observation ... We have not said "KnowledgeOS now knows rollback will succeed." We have established P(H\mid E_1)\approx0.905 under the assumptions of the model. That is statistical inference, not epistemic truth. Probability\neq KnowledgeState. This confirms the layered architecture from 2
b_rows_sample.statement: Confirms via the numerical example that Probability≠KnowledgeState — a computed posterior is statistical inference under model assumptions, not epistemic truth, validating the layered architecture from 25C.1.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Add genuinely independent evidence ... E_2 is an independently performed restore test. P(E_2\mid H)=0.90 and P(E_2\mid\neg H)=0.20. LR_2=4.5. Under the conditional-independence assumption LR_{12}=LR_1LR_2=42.75. P(H\mid E_1,E_2)\approx97.7\%. This demonstrates the legitimate case where independent e
b_rows_sample.statement: Computes the legitimate independent-evidence-combination case: LR12=LR1·LR2=42.75 yielding P(H|E1,E2)≈97.7%, demonstrating substantial legitimate confidence increase under genuine independence.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Now attack the independence assumption ... E_2 is simply a report generated from E_1. E_2=f(E_1). If we nevertheless calculate LR_{12}=LR_1LR_2, we manufacture certainty. This is mathematically wrong. IndependentEvidence must be established, not assumed.
b_rows_sample.statement: Shows that applying LR1·LR2 to a copied (E2=f(E1)) evidence pair manufactures false certainty mathematically — IndependentEvidence must be established, not assumed.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Perfect duplicate experiment ... E_2=E_1. Then P(H\mid E_1,E_2)=P(H\mid E_1). There should be no additional information. Aggregate(E,E)=Aggregate(E) for duplicate evidence. This confirms the idempotency requirement.
b_rows_sample.statement: Numerically confirms the idempotency requirement: a perfect duplicate provides zero additional posterior shift.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A surprising consequence ... the real input to inference is not \{E_1,E_2,\ldots,E_n\}. It is closer to Evidence Graph where we know relationships such as E_1\perp E_2 or E_2=f(E_1). This is not an implementation detail. It changes the mathematics of aggregation. ... Three cases ... Case A duplicate
b_rows_sample.statement: States that the true input to inference is the Evidence Graph (relationships, not a bare set), classifying three information-gain cases (duplicate=0, dependent=less than naive, independent=>0) as the beginning of an evidence-combination theory.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment — contradictory evidence ... E_3: Rollback test failed. P(E_3\mid H)=0.05 and P(E_3\mid\neg H)=0.80. LR_3=0.0625. 42.75\times0.0625=2.671875. P(H\mid E_1,E_2,E_3)\approx0.728. So the statistical model says approximately 72.8\%. ... But KnowledgeOS must not say merely "72.8%" ... Support=\
b_rows_sample.statement: Computes contradictory-evidence-adjusted posterior P(H|E1,E2,E3)≈72.8% while requiring the epistemic Support/Challenge structure be retained alongside the scalar — the critical result that the statistical result and qualitative epistemic state must coexist.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The statistical result and epistemic state coexist ... EpistemicAssessment + StatisticalInference. Proposition: Rollback will succeed. Evidence: E1 supports, E2 supports, E3 challenges. Conflict: true. Statistical model: P(H|E) = 0.728. Inference model: Bayesian. Dependency assumptions: E1 ⟂ E2. Thi
b_rows_sample.statement: Constructs a worked full record combining EpistemicAssessment and StatisticalInference (evidence roles, conflict flag, model, dependency assumptions), far richer than a bare confidence percentage.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment — source reliability ... E_3 comes from an uncalibrated test. We should not simply discard it. Instead its statistical model should represent P(E_3\mid H) and P(E_3\mid\neg H) appropriately. Reliability belongs in the model, not as an arbitrary score.
b_rows_sample.statement: States that source reliability belongs inside the statistical likelihood model (P(E|H), P(E|¬H)) rather than as an arbitrary bolt-on score.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment — one very strong evidence item versus many weak ones ... E_1 is a direct successful restore test. Then ten weak human statements. Naive counting says 10>1. KnowledgeOS must not use source count. EvidenceCount\neq EvidenceStrength.
b_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms EvidenceCount ≠ EvidenceStrength using a strong-single-test-vs-ten-weak-statements experiment.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment — common-cause dependence ... Infrastructure report, Operations report, Manager report all generated from the same monitoring dashboard. E_1,E_2,E_3 are highly correlated. There are three artifacts but approximately one underlying information source. This is exactly why lineage matters. .
b_rows_sample.statement: Contrasts a common-cause-dependent evidence set (three reports from one dashboard, one underlying source) with a genuinely independent evidence set (three separate physical systems), showing only the latter legitimately increases support.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The crucial requirement ... KnowledgeOS therefore needs to distinguish ArtifactMultiplicity from InformationMultiplicity. Three documents can represent one underlying fact. One experiment can generate several genuinely distinct observations. This is an epistemic identity problem, not merely a databa
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes ArtifactMultiplicity from InformationMultiplicity as an epistemic identity problem, not merely database deduplication.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment — evidence arriving sequentially ... After E_1: P(H)=0.905. After E_2: P(H)=0.977. After contradictory E_3: P(H)=0.728. This demonstrates Knowledge/evidence evolution can be non-monotonic. The numerical inference can increase and decrease as evidence arrives. ... But the evidence history
b_rows_sample.statement: Traces the full sequential posterior evolution (0.5→0.905→0.977→0.728), confirming non-monotonic inference alongside cumulative evidence history — InferenceState is revisable, EvidenceHistory is cumulative, matching 25A.3's earlier result.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment — retraction ... E_3 is later determined to be invalid. We do not erase the historical fact that at t_3, KnowledgeOS received E_3. Instead Status(E_3)=Invalid. Then recompute P(H\mid E_1,E_2,E_3^{invalid}). The inference can return toward 97.7%. But the history records why the inference c
b_rows_sample.statement: Works a retraction experiment where E3 is invalidated (not erased), triggering a recomputed posterior returning toward 97.7% while the history records why.

b_rows_sample.anchor: This produces an important invariant ... I_{t+1}=Infer(K_{t+1},M). If evidence is retracted K_{t+1}=Revision(K_t,E^{invalid}). Then I_{t+1} must be recalculated. Inference is a projection of KnowledgeState, not the KnowledgeState itself. This is an important architectural principle.
b_rows_sample.statement: States the invariant Inference is a projection of KnowledgeState, not the KnowledgeState itself — requiring recalculation whenever the underlying KnowledgeState is revised (e.g. via retraction).

b_rows_sample.anchor: This changes how we should model probabilities ... We should not store only P(H)=0.728. We should store InferenceResult=(H,Probability,Model,ModelVersion,InputKnowledgeSnapshot,Assumptions). Hypothesis: H, Probability: 0.728, Model: Bayesian, ModelVersion: 1.2, KnowledgeSnapshot: K17, Assumptions: E
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a full reproducible InferenceResult=(H,Probability,Model,ModelVersion,InputKnowledgeSnapshot,Assumptions) record instead of storing a bare probability.

b_rows_sample.anchor: This is extremely important for KnowledgeOS ... Why did KnowledgeOS say rollback had a 72.8% probability? We should be able to answer Because K_{17} + Model_{1.2} + Assumptions_{X} \Rightarrow0.728. This is much stronger than "The AI estimated 72.8%."
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues the InferenceResult record enables answering 'why did KnowledgeOS say 72.8%?' with a precise reconstruction (snapshot+model+assumptions), far stronger than 'the AI estimated it'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: We now have a candidate inference contract ... Inference(K,H,M,C) \rightarrow R where K = knowledge snapshot; H = hypothesis; M = mathematical model; C = assumptions/context; R = inference result. This is a clean DDD/application boundary.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the inference contract Inference(K,H,M,C)→R as a clean DDD/application boundary.

b_rows_sample.anchor: What should happen if the model is inappropriate? ... Architecture Board approval is mandatory. Trying to calculate P(ApprovalRequired) is usually the wrong operation. The appropriate reasoning may be RuleEvaluation(K,Policy) \rightarrow Required. NotEveryPropositionRequiresStatisticalInference. Thi
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues NotEveryPropositionRequiresStatisticalInference (a normative approval requirement should use RuleEvaluation, not probability), reinforcing the rejection of a universal Bayesian kernel, and defines four reasoning modes (Deductive/Normative, Statistical, Causal, Semantic/Fuzzy).

group_evidence.why_grouped: labels share the notation 'A1..A10'

a_rows_sample.anchor: [PROP] A successful epistemic inquiry may contain a transition event at which its applicable closure conditions become satisfied. Candidate: ClosureEvent(Q,t) ... But we have not established that KnowledgeOS requires such an event. That needs an experiment.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes the candidate object ClosureEvent(Q,t), sitting between the epistemic-interaction process and the resulting successor state (K_t -> Inquiry -> EpistemicInteraction -> ClosureEvent -> K_{t+1}), explicitly not yet established as required by KnowledgeOS and flagged as needing a dedicated experiment.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Case A: No one investigated. Case B: Evidence insufficient. Case C: Evidence contradictory. Case D: Theory cannot evaluate the requirement. Case E: Inquiry genuinely closed. All of these could superficially collapse into some generic 'not known yet.' But they are structurally different.
a_rows_sample.statement: Connects to Experiment G's finding that EVal={T,F,U} is insufficient: five structurally distinct cases (no investigation, insufficient evidence, contradictory evidence, theory cannot evaluate, genuinely closed) could all superficially collapse into a generic 'not known yet' but must be kept distinct, yielding Closure != Evaluation Value and ClosureStatus != EpistemicTruth.

a_rows_sample.anchor: This metaphor must not currently be used to establish: A new KnowledgeOS primitive called Orgasm / A kernel operator / Orgasm = Reconciliation / A new truth value / Zero = closure (refuted) / Closure = knowledge (not established) / Knowledge = truth (already separated) / Proposal/Challenge as DDD aggregates (too early) / Two agents as a required architecture (not supported).
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicit scope-limiting ruling on what the sexual-metaphor document does NOT establish: no new primitive 'Orgasm', no kernel operator, no Orgasm=Reconciliation equation, no new truth value, Zero=closure is refuted as oversimplification, Closure=Knowledge is unestablished, Knowledge=Truth remains separated, Proposal/Challenge as DDD aggregates is premature, and a required two-agent architecture is unsupported.

a_rows_sample.anchor: I would therefore NOT immediately create 'Epistemic Orgasm.' I would preserve it as a source metaphor/hypothesis, but create the research abstraction: Epistemic Closure Event ... Then test: Proposal->Challenge->Evidence->Assessment->Reconciliation->ClosureEvent->SuccessorState ... Can Closure Event be distinguished from reconciliation, determination, knowledge attribution, truth, and Zero closure?
a_rows_sample.statement: Governance decision: retain 'epistemic orgasm' only as a source metaphor, formalize the research abstraction Epistemic Closure Event, and pose the critical experiment as whether Closure Event can be distinguished from reconciliation, determination, knowledge attribution, truth, and Zero closure -- if yes the metaphor generated a real theoretical distinction, if no it is merely a colorful redescription.

a_rows_sample.anchor: I would now insert this after the Zero Boundary work, not before it ... New candidate branch: After Boundary semantics become sufficiently stable: Epistemic Interaction / Closure Event experiment. Then ask whether it actually adds explanatory power.
a_rows_sample.statement: Revises the research TODO sequence to Zero->Boundary->Inquiry->Interaction->Evaluation->Reconciliation->Closure?->Successor State, inserting the Epistemic Interaction/Closure Event experiment after Zero Boundary work stabilizes rather than before, with Closure deliberately left unresolved pending that experiment.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose K_t is determined. We declare Orgasm_t. Then new evidence arrives E_{t+1} and invalidates the determination. ... The metaphor survives if Orgasm_t is understood as closure at time t. It fails if orgasm means permanently complete knowledge. Therefore: EpistemicOrgasm_t must be temporal and revisable.
a_rows_sample.statement: Falsification test: if a determination is declared closed (Orgasm_t) and later evidence invalidates it (K_{t+1}!=K_t), the ClosureEvent metaphor survives only if understood as closure-at-time-t (temporal and revisable), and fails if it means permanently complete knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: An epistemic system may contain a distinct closure event in which a proposal/challenge process has reached a sufficiently reconciled and inquiry-adequate condition, producing a new epistemic state, without identifying that event with Zero, Truth, Determination, or Knowledge. ... The formal candidate name should be: EpistemicClosureEvent.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the formal research question: can a distinct EpistemicClosureEvent (formal name, replacing the metaphorical 'Orgasm' label) be identified where a proposal/challenge process reaches sufficient reconciliation and inquiry-adequacy, producing a new epistemic state, without collapsing into Zero, Truth, Determination, or Knowledge?

a_rows_sample.anchor: Model A - Closure as state: Closed_t(K). Model B - Closure as transition event: ClosureEvent_t: K_t -> K_(t+1). ... If closure can later be revised, determine whether ClosureEvent_t is historical and irreversible as an event, while K_(t+1) remains revisable.
a_rows_sample.statement: Requires testing two competing formal models of closure -- Model A, closure as a state predicate Closed_t(K); Model B, closure as a transition event ClosureEvent_t: K_t -> K_{t+1} -- and, if closure can later be revised, whether the event itself remains historical/irreversible while the resulting state K_{t+1} remains revisable (HistoricalClosure != CurrentClosure; StateRevision != EventDeletion).

a_rows_sample.anchor: A question can be closed for inquiry Q while another inquiry Q' exposes additional gaps. ... Closure(Q,t) = true, ZeroLens(K_t,Q') ≠ empty. If this is possible, record it as evidence that closure is inquiry-relative and does not imply global completeness.
a_rows_sample.statement: Critical Zero-separation test: whether Closure(Q,t)=true can coexist with ZeroLens(K_t,Q')!=empty for a different inquiry Q', which if possible would establish that closure is inquiry-relative and does not imply global completeness.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Test: ClosureEvent ≠ KnowledgeAttribution and Determination ≠ KnowledgeAttribution. Construct false-but-well-supported proposals. If closure occurs without truth, this must NOT automatically produce knowledge. Record: [EXP] Closure can be epistemically successful without being factive knowledge.
a_rows_sample.statement: Requires testing ClosureEvent!=KnowledgeAttribution and Determination!=KnowledgeAttribution via constructed false-but-well-supported proposals; if closure occurs without truth this must not automatically produce knowledge, recordable only if witnessed as [EXP] closure can be epistemically successful without being factive knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Does an epistemic system contain a distinct closure event ... without identifying that event with Zero, Truth, Determination or Knowledge? Answer: yes for the distinctions, no for the primitiveness. All five conditions separate; the event itself is derivable as a predicate but carries one thing no predicate does.
a_rows_sample.statement: Headline answer to the KR-CLOSURE research question: yes for the distinctions (Balanced/Reconciled/Determined/Known/Closed all separate), no for primitiveness (the closure event is derivable as a predicate); the event nonetheless carries something no predicate carries -- historical irreversibility.

a_rows_sample.anchor: {Balanced, Reconciled, Determined, Known, Closed} ... 10 of 10 distinguishable. Two directed cells initially had no witness; both were investigated rather than reported as implications.
a_rows_sample.statement: The pairwise distinction matrix over {Balanced, Reconciled, Determined, Known, Closed} yields 10 of 10 pairs distinguishable by constructed witness; two directed cells (Balanced-and-not-Reconciled, Known-and-not-Determined) initially lacked a witness and were investigated rather than defaulted to an implication.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Balanced ∧ ¬Reconciled -- a catalogue gap, not an implication. Negative-control case 2 (support .8 + contradict .8) is the witness: balanced, not reconciled. Repaired.
a_rows_sample.statement: The missing Balanced-and-not-Reconciled witness was a catalogue gap rather than a genuine implication: negative-control case 2 (support 0.8 + contradict 0.8) supplies it (balanced, not reconciled) once identified.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Known ∧ ¬Determined -- constructible, but forbidden by the attribution policy. ... [EXP] Known ⇒ Determined is policy-relative, not conceptual. It is a property of Γ's attribution policy, and it disappears when the policy is relaxed.
a_rows_sample.statement: [EXP]: Known=>Determined is policy-relative, not conceptual -- a Known-without-Determined state is constructible but forbidden under the 'justified-unique' attribution policy while reachable under 'justified-any' (confirmed by the -C policy sweep), so the apparent implication is a property of Gamma's attribution policy, not a conceptual necessity.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A -- Closed_t(K) as a state: true at t, false after new evidence at t+1. B -- ClosureEvent_t: K_t -> K_{t+1}: occurred at t, still occurred after t+1. Closure-as-state is refuted by temporal revision; closure-as-event is not. ... This does not make the event permanent truth ... a system can close on a falsehood.
a_rows_sample.statement: [EXP]: closure-as-state (Closed_t(K)) is refuted by temporal revision (true at t, false after new evidence at t+1), while closure-as-event (ClosureEvent_t: K_t->K_{t+1}) survives (occurred at t, still occurred after t+1) -- the event is a historical fact remaining true of the past even though K_{t+1} remains revisable; this does not make the event permanent truth, since a system can close on a falsehood (the B1 factivity counterexample still stands).

a_rows_sample.anchor: ClosureEvent ... DERIVABLE AS A PREDICATE -- Determined ∧ Adequate. But §4 shows it carries a historical record that neither conjunct carries. So: derivable as a predicate, not as an event [PROP]. ... The predicate adds nothing; the event adds irreversibility. Whether irreversibility is kernel structure or an audit-log concern is [OPEN] -- and it is a DDD question, not a mathematical one.
a_rows_sample.statement: [PROP]/[OPEN]: ClosureEvent is derivable as a predicate (Determined AND Adequate) but that predicate carries no historical record, while the event does -- so ClosureEvent is derivable as a predicate but not as an event; whether the irreversibility the event carries is kernel structure or merely an audit-log concern is left [OPEN] as a DDD boundary question (History vs Kernel), not a mathematical one.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Decide whether event-irreversibility is kernel structure or an audit concern. It is the only thing ClosureEvent contributes that its defining conjunction does not, and the question is a DDD boundary question -- History vs Kernel -- not a mathematical one. It is also cheap: it needs no new simulation, only a context-map decision.
a_rows_sample.statement: Recommended next step: decide, as a DDD context-map decision (History vs Kernel boundary) rather than a new simulation, whether ClosureEvent's irreversibility belongs to kernel structure or is merely an audit-log concern -- the only contribution ClosureEvent makes beyond its defining conjunction (Determined AND Adequate).

a_rows_sample.anchor: I currently lean strongly toward: ClosureEvent ∈ History, not Kernel, because the experiment found ClosureEvent as predicate is derivable from Determined ∧ Adequate, while the additional property is 'this closure occurred at t.' That sounds fundamentally historical.
a_rows_sample.statement: Preliminary position: ClosureEvent likely belongs to History, not Kernel, since the derivable predicate (Determined AND Adequate) is fully kernel-explicable while the additional property ('this closure occurred at t') is fundamentally historical -- Closed(K_t,Q) as a current epistemic predicate vs ClosureEvent(t,Q,K_t,K_{t+1}) as a historical transition record.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Current State ≠ Historical Transition and therefore: K_t ≠ History_{≤t}. History records what happened to the epistemic state, not necessarily what the current epistemic state is. ... irreversibility may belong to event identity, not epistemic computation.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a general principle: Current State != Historical Transition, hence K_t != History_{<=t} -- history records what happened to the epistemic state, not what the current state is; the kernel operates on state/transition semantics while history preserves the fact that a transition occurred, so irreversibility may belong to event identity rather than epistemic computation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A -- Pure audit: ClosureEvent ∈ Audit/History. The kernel does not need to know that closure happened. B -- Domain history: ClosureEvent ∈ DomainHistory. ... C -- Kernel structure: ClosureEvent ∈ 𝒦. ... I think C is currently unlikely, but we should not assume A versus B.
a_rows_sample.statement: Refines the History-vs-Kernel question into three possibilities for where ClosureEvent belongs: (A) pure audit/infrastructure history the kernel need not know about, (B) domain history -- a genuine domain event because later domain behavior may depend on it, (C) kernel structure itself; judges C currently unlikely but declines to assume between A and B.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Reconciliation != Knowledge and Orgasm = transition event and Knowledge = resulting epistemic state ... E_t --Reconciliation--> OrgasmEvent_t --Attribution--> K_{t+1}
b_rows_sample.statement: Reframes 'orgasm' from a static balanced state to a discrete transition event (ClosureEvent) mapping an epistemic state to its successor via reconciliation and attribution, explicitly separating reconciliation from knowledge.

b_rows_sample.anchor: +0.8 + (-0.8) = 0 ... A The evidence genuinely balances. B The evidence is contradictory. C The evidence is insufficient. D The evidence is incomparable. E ... double-counted. F ... concerns different times. All six produce something that looks like zero. ... Numeric zero != Epistemic closure.
b_rows_sample.statement: Delivers the decisive negative test: at least six distinct and non-equivalent epistemic conditions (genuine balance, contradiction, insufficiency, incomparability, dependent double-counted evidence, temporally-distinct claims) all produce apparent numeric zero, so numeric zero cannot be identified with epistemic closure.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Orgasm(Q,t) <=> Closure(Q,t) and Reconciled(Q,t) and Adequate(Q,t) and Stable(Q,t) but Closure, Reconciled, and Stable are themselves currently open concepts. So we should not pretend we have solved them.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a research-hypothesis (not definition) formal criterion for an 'epistemic orgasm'/closure event conjoining four currently-open sub-concepts, explicitly flagging that none of the four is yet solved.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KR-ORGASM-2026-09-02 ... Can epistemic orgasm be operationalized as a closure event generated by proposal-challenge-reconciliation dynamics without collapsing Zero, determination, truth, or knowledge into one state? ... 15 test cases ... If they collapse into one state, the metaphor is too crude.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a falsification-oriented KR-ORGASM research track with 15 named adversarial test cases, whose success criterion is whether Balanced/Reconciled/Determined/Known/Closed remain distinguishable while dynamically linked by the closure event.

group_evidence.why_grouped: working_label token overlap Jaccard=0.60 (shared tokens: ['closure', 'epistemic', 'event'])

a_rows_sample.anchor: The document repeatedly asserts K_Kernel ≡ Yoni and finally: 'The Kernel is the Yoni.' This is exactly the kind of promotion our research discipline is supposed to prevent. ... There is currently no structure-preserving correspondence showing Yoni ≅ K. Therefore the correct classification is: Yoni [EXT] → Kernel [PROP], not: Yoni = Kernel.
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects the source document's central claim 'Kernel = Yoni' as an unjustified premature promotion: no structure-preserving correspondence (Yoni cong Kernel) has been shown, and KR-2026-09-01/KR-CLOSURE have left kernel minimality explicitly blocked -- the correct classification is Yoni[EXT] feeding into a Kernel[PROP] hypothesis, not an identity.

a_rows_sample.anchor: It uses 'Kernel' to mean: A. Knowledge Space ... B. Epistemic State ... C. Kernel ... operations that transform the field ... D. History / transitions ... 'rhythms' ... Knowledge Space ≠ Epistemic State ≠ Kernel ≠ History.
a_rows_sample.statement: Identifies the source document's central defect: it uses the single word 'Kernel' to mean four theoretically distinct things -- (A) Knowledge Space (the field where epistemic activity occurs), (B) Epistemic State (current field condition), (C) Kernel (operations transforming the field), (D) History/transitions ('rhythms') -- and that its notation 'K=Knowledge State, O=Operations, Sigma=Epistemic State, T=Transitions' is not a harmless simplification but a collapse of four distinct layers requiring Knowledge Space!=Epistemic State!=Kernel!=History.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Not: Kernel = Yoni but: Yoni is a philosophical lens for the epistemic field in which differentiated contributions interact and from which subsequent epistemic states emerge. Then: Yoni [EXT] → EpistemicField [PROP] and: Kernel [OPEN] ⊆/acts on EpistemicField [PROP].
a_rows_sample.statement: Rescues the source document by re-centering its thesis: Yoni is a lens for an EpistemicField (a relational space of differentiated interacting contributions), and the Kernel (still [OPEN]) acts on or is a subset of that field, rather than being identical to it -- formalized as F_t = Epistemic Field at t, with Kernel: (F_t,E_t,Q_t,S_t,M_t) -> F_{t+1}.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Receiving → Assessing → Reconciling → Generating → Receiving again ... resembles our established temporal view: K_t --Θ--> K_{t+1} and: K_{t+1} → ZeroLens → new inquiry → new evidence. ... Epistemic systems are generative and recursively self-renewing. That is a legitimate [PROP] worth investigating.
a_rows_sample.statement: Rescues the source document's cyclic Receiving->Assessing->Reconciling->Generating->Receiving-again pattern as matching the established K_t-Theta->K_{t+1}->ZeroLens->new-inquiry cycle, extracting the [PROP] hypothesis that 'epistemic systems are generative and recursively self-renewing.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: Lord = Yoni's potential and: SārathiLens = Yoni's guidance. ... They should therefore not be interpreted as internal 'organs' or components of a Yoni-Kernel. They are functional lenses over the epistemic system.
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects treating Lord and Sarathi as internal 'organs'/components of a Yoni-Kernel, retaining the existing cleaner formalizations Lord(K_t,Delta_t,Q_t)->CandidateSet and Guide(K_t,Delta_t,A^act,Q,C)->Preference as functional lenses over the epistemic system, not Yoni sub-parts.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Assert, Retract, Supersede, Merge, Support, Refute, Assess, Resolve ... we should not add these to the kernel merely because the metaphor suggests them. ... So the document's operational list should be treated as: [PROP] candidate epistemic capabilities not kernel operators.
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects promoting the source document's eight-item operator list (Assert, Retract, Supersede, Merge, Support, Refute, Assess, Resolve) directly into the kernel, citing the KR-CLOSURE finding that Proposal-generation/Argument-relation/Reconciliation are derivable while Challenge-generation/Evidence-assessment remain unresolved and Closure-detection is only predicate-derivable -- the list should be treated as [PROP] candidate epistemic capabilities, not settled kernel operators.

a_rows_sample.anchor: State → Transition → Event → History. A closure event is not merely another state. ... Epistemic Field [box with Proposal, Challenge, Evidence, Arguments, Alternatives] → Kernel → K_t → K_t+1 → [Domain Events, History].
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a revised architectural picture distinguishing State->Transition->Event->History as four distinct layers (a closure event is not merely another state), with the Epistemic Field (Proposal/Challenge/Evidence/Arguments/Alternatives) feeding the Kernel's K_t->K_{t+1} transition, which in turn feeds Domain Events and History.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Difference → Interaction → Transformation → Emergence. ... Proposal ≠ Challenge creates a relation. Then: Proposal + Challenge + Evidence creates an Argument Field. ... ArgumentField → Reconciliation/Determination and potentially → ClosureEvent → E_{t+1}. Then Zero exposes the next boundary. So the system is not a static repository of knowledge. It is a generative epistemic process.
a_rows_sample.statement: Identifies the deepest recoverable pattern in the source metaphor: Difference->Interaction->Transformation->Emergence, instantiated as Proposal!=Challenge creating a relation, Proposal+Challenge+Evidence creating an ArgumentField, which undergoes Reconciliation/Determination and potentially ClosureEvent->E_{t+1}, after which Zero exposes the next boundary -- KnowledgeOS as a generative epistemic process rather than a static repository, judged the strongest contribution of the Yoni metaphor.

a_rows_sample.anchor: What I would retain: [EXT] Yoni as receptive/generative field. [PROP] Epistemic field as relational rather than merely a collection of facts. [PROP] Knowledge production as interaction and transformation. [PROP] Multiple epistemic roles can participate. [PROP] New epistemic state as the 'offspring'. [EXP+EXT] Closure as event rather than permanent state. [PROP] The field can recursively generate the next inquiry.
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicit retain-list from the source document, each item tagged with an evidence-level marker: Yoni-as-field [EXT], relational epistemic field [PROP], interaction/transformation-based knowledge production [PROP], multiple epistemic roles [PROP], offspring-as-new-state [PROP], closure-as-event [EXP+EXT], recursive field self-renewal [PROP].

a_rows_sample.anchor: Reject: Kernel=Yoni. Reject: Knowledge=Offspring. Reject: Truth=Offspring. Reject: Reconciliation=Orgasm=Closure. Reject: Balanced=Reconciled. Reject: all contradictions are reconciled. Reject: all epistemic activity occurs inside the Kernel. ... the closure experiment demonstrated that scalar balance is not merely insufficient -- it can conceal materially different epistemic structures.
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicit reject-list of seven overreaching claims from the source document (Kernel=Yoni, Knowledge=Offspring, Truth=Offspring, Reconciliation=Orgasm=Closure, Balanced=Reconciled, 'all contradictions are reconciled', 'all epistemic activity occurs inside the Kernel'), grounded in the closure experiment's finding that scalar balance can conceal materially different epistemic structures.

a_rows_sample.anchor: [EXT/PROP] The Yoni metaphor represents the epistemic field as a receptive and generative relational space in which differentiated epistemic contributions ... interact and transform the current epistemic state. It does not establish that the Yoni is the KnowledgeOS kernel. ... Field → Interaction → Argument Field → Assessment → Reconciliation → ClosureEvent → New EpistemicState followed by New EpistemicState → ZeroLens → New Boundary → New Inquiry.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes the revised research-record thesis: the Yoni metaphor is a lens for a receptive/generative relational epistemic field, explicitly not the kernel; supplies a corrected 8-stage metaphorical cycle: Field->Interaction->ArgumentField->Assessment->Reconciliation->ClosureEvent->NewEpistemicState->ZeroLens->NewBoundary->NewInquiry.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The semantic structure is richer than any single summary predicate. The Zero Lens experiment found this with boundary conditions. The closure experiment found it with argument relations. The Yoni metaphor independently points toward the same structure-over-projection phenomenon. That convergence is worth investigating -- but it is not yet a theorem.
a_rows_sample.statement: Notes a three-way independent convergence on the same 'structure over projection' phenomenon (semantic structure richer than any single summary predicate): the Zero Lens experiment (boundary conditions), the closure experiment (argument relations), and now the Yoni metaphor (independently) -- explicitly marked as a convergence worth investigating, not yet a theorem.

a_rows_sample.anchor: | Field | Kernel | | Contains potential | Actualizes | | Relates contributions | Transforms state | | Holds possibilities | Determines current |
a_rows_sample.statement: Sharpens the Field-vs-Kernel distinction into a three-row contrast table: Field contains potential / Kernel actualizes; Field relates contributions / Kernel transforms state; Field holds possibilities / Kernel determines the current state.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Kernel = Yoni is not accepted. Yoni is [EXT] -- a philosophical lens. There is no structure-preserving correspondence Yoni ≅ 𝒦 ... Also in force: Zero is a lens, not a state producer (Zero Concept v1.2 §3: Zero ≠ K_t).
a_rows_sample.statement: Confirms as standing discipline (citing the corpus's own S2448 critique) that Kernel=Yoni is not accepted and Zero is a lens, not a state producer (Zero != K_t per Zero Concept v1.2 section 3), before running the empirical test.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS = Yoni × Zero × Sārathi is a category error. Yoni/Zero/Sārathi are each lenses [EXT]; KnowledgeOS is a system -- bounded contexts + kernel. Three instruments on the right, a system on the left. v1.2's constitutional separation forbids exactly this: a lens is an instrument for examining the domain, not a component of it.
a_rows_sample.statement: [NEG]: refutes 'KnowledgeOS = Yoni x Zero x Sarathi' as a category error -- three lenses (each [EXT] or already-established examining instruments) cannot equal the system (bounded contexts + kernel) they are used to examine; this is the same instrument-into-domain overreach already identified as 'Kernel=Yoni', recurring in the final equation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Two of the four refutations are the same defect ... Kernel = Yoni, the final KnowledgeOS = Yoni × Zero × Sārathi equation, and §3.3's Zero-as-state-producer are all instrument-into-domain promotions. ... [PROP] A cheap standing check: any proposed equation whose left side is a domain object and whose right side contains a lens is a category error by construction. That is statically checkable against the declared lens register.
a_rows_sample.statement: Identifies that three of the refuted claims (Kernel=Yoni, KnowledgeOS=Yoni x Zero x Sarathi, and Zero-as-state-producer) share one defect -- promoting an examining instrument into the domain it examines -- and proposes a cheap standing static check: any equation whose left side is a domain object and right side contains a lens is a category error by construction, statically checkable against a declared lens register, which would have flagged all three before they were written.

a_rows_sample.anchor: a lens may observe, transform or interpret a domain object only according to its declared contract; it must not become the domain object merely by appearing in an equation that names that object. Statically: reject DomainObject = f(Lens). Lens register ... Zero 1262, Lord 407, Krishna 198, Yoni 56, Sārathi 49, Sarathi 3, Buddhi 1. (Linga never appears with a Lens suffix -- it is proposed, not yet registered.)
a_rows_sample.statement: Implements the S2453-proposed static category check as a rule (reject DomainObject=f(Lens)) plus a derived lens register from corpus occurrence counts (Zero 1262, Lord 407, Krishna 198, Yoni 56, Sarathi 49/3, Buddhi 1); notes Linga never appears with a Lens suffix and is not yet registered.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 37 raw hits, 11 live assertions ... LIVE ASSERTION 11, NEGATED-IN-CONTEXT 12, QUOTED-IN-CRITIQUE 7, QUOTED-IN-AUDIT 7. The naive count of 37 overstates it by 26. ... The check is only usable with this classification.
a_rows_sample.statement: Running the category check against the corpus yields 37 raw textual hits but only 11 classify as LIVE ASSERTION (the rest are NEGATED-IN-CONTEXT, QUOTED-IN-CRITIQUE, or QUOTED-IN-AUDIT -- the corpus quoting the error to reject it); the naive raw count overstates true violations by 26, and the check is only usable once this four-way classification is applied.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS = Sañjaya + Sārathi (and variants) 6 ... One dominant pattern accounts for 6 of 11, and Yoni × Zero × Sārathi -- the equation just refuted in N -- is the same pattern's newest instance. [EXP] The category error is recurrent, not incidental, and the check localizes it to eleven places.
a_rows_sample.statement: [EXP]: one dominant equation pattern ('KnowledgeOS = Sanjaya + Sarathi' and variants) accounts for 6 of the 11 live category-error violations, and the 'Yoni x Zero x Sarathi' equation refuted in S2453 is simply the newest instance of the same recurring pattern -- the category error is recurrent across the corpus, not an isolated incident, and the check localizes it to exactly eleven places.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Sañjaya is not in the register because it never appears with a Lens suffix. If it is a lens -- and it is used as one -- the six dominant hits are more clearly category errors, not less. Registering the lens vocabulary is a prerequisite for the check to be complete. [OPEN]
a_rows_sample.statement: Notes Sanjaya is omitted from the derived lens register purely because it never carries a 'Lens' suffix, even though it is used as a lens in the corpus -- meaning the six dominant category-error hits are undercounted, not overcounted, and a declared (not occurrence-derived) lens register is a prerequisite for completeness, left [OPEN].

b_rows_sample.anchor: The deeper interpretation is not two people having an epistemic interaction. It is a field in which multiple epistemic agents contribute, challenge, transform, and recombine representations until a new state emerges. ... Epistemic Field = {agents, propositions, evidence, relations, interpretations, standards}.
b_rows_sample.statement: Generalizes the two-pole (A+/B-) interaction model into an Epistemic Field = {agents, propositions, evidence, relations, interpretations, standards} in which n agents simultaneously propose, support, challenge, reinterpret, qualify, introduce evidence/alternatives, discover gaps, or revise positions.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Architect: proposes migration. Operations: challenges operational feasibility. Security: introduces security evidence. Finance: introduces cost constraints. Developer: challenges implementation assumptions. Management: introduces business requirements. Infrastructure: provides empirical observations. There isn't one 'male' pole and one 'female' pole. There is a multi-agent epistemic field.
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked example: a 'migrate Nexus to new platform?' question involves seven distinct role-holders (Architect, Operations, Security, Finance, Developer, Management, Infrastructure) each contributing differently, illustrating that real epistemic inquiry is a multi-agent field, not a two-pole opposition.

b_rows_sample.anchor: AF_t(Q) = (V_t, E_t, R_t, 𝒜_t, C_t) where V_t = epistemic agents, E_t = evidence, R_t = relations between contributions, 𝒜_t = alternatives/hypotheses, C_t = context. That is much closer to the KnowledgeOS problem.
b_rows_sample.statement: Candidate formalization of the multi-agent argument field: AF_t(Q)=(V_t,E_t,R_t,A_t,C_t) with V_t agents, E_t evidence, R_t relations between contributions, A_t alternatives/hypotheses, C_t context.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose three people contribute: A: H, B: ¬H, C: H'. The situation is no longer +n + (-n) = 0. Instead: {H, ¬H, H'} with relationships between them ... How does the system represent and assess a field of competing epistemic contributions?
b_rows_sample.statement: Three-contributor example (A:H, B:not-H, C:H') shows the situation is not scalar cancellation +n+(-n)=0 but a structured set {H,not-H,H'} with typed relations (supports, undermines, alternative, qualifies) between propositions and evidence, reframing the KnowledgeOS problem as representing/assessing a field of competing contributions.

b_rows_sample.anchor: N-Agent Epistemic Interaction with N=1,2,3,... ask: What is the smallest number of epistemically differentiated roles required for the interaction to produce something that cannot be represented by an isolated epistemic state? ... Person count is probably not fundamental. What matters is differentiated epistemic function.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes replacing the two-person KR-ORGASM experiment's fixed N=2 with an N-Agent Epistemic Interaction test (N=1,2,3,4+) asking the minimum number of differentiated epistemic roles needed to produce something an isolated epistemic state cannot represent, with the working hypothesis that person count is not fundamental -- differentiated epistemic function is what matters.

b_rows_sample.anchor: If there is only one completely undifferentiated state: X=X there is no interaction. But epistemic inquiry requires distinctions: H≠H', Evidence≠Hypothesis, Observer≠Observed, Question≠Answer, Proposal≠Challenge, CurrentState≠IdealState. ... Difference → Interaction → Transformation → NewState.
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues difference is a prerequisite for knowledge generation: an undifferentiated state (X=X) permits no interaction, whereas epistemic inquiry requires distinctions (H!=H', Evidence!=Hypothesis, Observer!=Observed, Question!=Answer, Proposal!=Challenge, CurrentState!=IdealState); connects this to the Zero Lens (which identifies boundaries/differences) via the chain Difference -> Interaction -> Transformation -> NewState.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge generation is relational rather than purely individual. ... A KnowledgeOS epistemic state may be transformed through interactions among multiple differentiated epistemic roles ... E_t --Interaction(A,E,H,S,M,Q)--> E_{t+1} with possible closure event CE_t: E_t → E_{t+1}. And only afterward KnowledgeAttribution(E_{t+1}) can determine whether some part of the resulting state qualifies as knowledge.
b_rows_sample.statement: Adopts as a research hypothesis (not canonical) 'knowledge generation is relational rather than purely individual': an epistemic state transforms via interaction among multiple differentiated roles, E_t -Interaction(agents,evidence,hypotheses,standards,model,question)-> E_{t+1}, with a possible closure event CE_t:E_t->E_{t+1}, after which KnowledgeAttribution(E_{t+1}) separately determines whether any part qualifies as knowledge.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Add a major research track: Multi-Agent Epistemic Interaction Experiment. Test: N=1,2,3,N and distinguish: Person ≠ Agent ≠ Epistemic Role. ... Does epistemic closure require interpersonal plurality, or only epistemic differentiation? ... Epistemic plurality may itself be a condition of some forms of knowledge generation.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a Multi-Agent Epistemic Interaction Experiment track testing N=1,2,3,N and distinguishing Person != Agent != EpistemicRole, posing the research question of whether epistemic closure requires interpersonal plurality or only epistemic differentiation; if N=1 self-challenge cannot reproduce N=2 transformations, epistemic plurality may itself be a condition of some forms of knowledge generation -- explicitly framed as a testable hypothesis generated by the metaphor, not proved by it.

group_evidence.why_grouped: labels share the alias 'Epistemic Field'

a_rows_sample.anchor: one may not be in a position to know what one's own rational requirements or evidence are. ... Epistemic Property not=> Accessible(Epistemic Property) ... Knowledge(p) not=> Knowledge(Knowledge(p)) ... Eval(P) may be undefined or epistemically inaccessible even when P has a determinate truth value.
a_rows_sample.statement: States epistemic non-transparency as the strongest single Williamson contribution: an epistemic property (knowledge, evidence, rational requirement) can hold without being accessible to the subject/evaluator, giving a formal reason Sat/Eval_c must not be assumed luminous and must not be confused with truth. Status: [DERIVED - very strong].

a_rows_sample.anchor: anti-luminosity: roughly, the assumption that whenever a condition obtains, one is automatically in a position to know that it obtains. His argument uses reliability, limited discrimination and sorites-style reasoning. ... EvidenceExists(e) not=> EvaluatorCanEstablish(EvidenceExists(e)) ... Zero(K)=0 not=> Known(Zero(K)=0). This is very important for Zero.
a_rows_sample.statement: Applies the non-transparency principle specifically to Zero and consistency/completeness: EvidenceExists(e) not=> EvaluatorCanEstablish(EvidenceExists(e)); Consistent(K) not=> Known(Consistent(K)); Complete(K) not=> Known(Complete(K)); Zero(K)=0 not=> Known(Zero(K)=0) -- i.e. even if a knowledge base actually has zero gap, the system may be unable to know that it has zero gap.

a_rows_sample.anchor: EPISTEMIC LIMITS, ACCESSIBILITY AND KNOWLEDGE STANDING ... EL.1 Factivity [DECIDED/REINFORCED] ... EL.7 Structural Unknowability [PROP — strong research candidate] ... EL.8 Assertion Responsibility [PROP]
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes an 8-section theory addition 'EPISTEMIC LIMITS, ACCESSIBILITY AND KNOWLEDGE STANDING': EL.1 Factivity [DECIDED/REINFORCED], EL.2 Epistemic Non-Transparency [DERIVED], EL.3 Knowledge Iteration [DERIVED], EL.4 Evidence Relativity [PROP], EL.5 Margin of Error [PROP], EL.6 Accessibility (distinguishing Truth/Knowability/Accessibility/ActualKnowledge) [DERIVED], EL.7 Structural Unknowability [PROP-strong], EL.8 Assertion Responsibility [PROP], consolidating this file's individual candidates into one proposed section.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Do not adopt KnowledgeOS = Williamson's epistemology ... Do not adopt Knowledge = Evidence ... He explicitly says the equation does not amount to an analysis of either concept. ... Do not adopt Sat = Knowledge ... Confidence = Margin ... Unknown = Unknowable ... Contr = Epistemic inconsistency ... Zero = Structural unknowability
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicit rejection list of seven tempting imports: KnowledgeOS=Williamson's-epistemology, Knowledge=Evidence (noting Williamson himself says his E=K thesis is not an analysis of either concept), Sat=Knowledge, Confidence=Margin, Unknown=Unknowable, Contr=EpistemicInconsistency, Zero=StructuralUnknowability -- these remain separate concepts.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A condition C is defined to be luminous if and only if: For every case alpha, if in alpha C obtains, then in alpha one is in a position to know that C obtains. ... The Sorites-Style Argument [feeling cold at dawn to hot at noon] ... Therefore the condition 'one feels cold' is not luminous.
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives the formal definition of luminosity (a condition C is luminous iff whenever C obtains one is in a position to know it obtains) and the full sorites-style anti-luminosity argument (feeling-cold-at-dawn-to-hot-at-noon, imperceptible per-step changes) proving virtually no mental state is luminous, including love/hope examples generalizing beyond feeling-cold; grounds the epistemic-non-transparency principle with its original formal source material.

a_rows_sample.anchor: if we combine the argument with the principle that one is always in a position to know what one's evidence is, the upshot is that one has exactly the same evidence in an ordinary case and its sceptical counterpart. ... Luminous conditions are trivial. Since mental states are non-luminous, the sceptical argument fails. ... KnowledgeOS should not adopt a phenomenal conception of evidence.
a_rows_sample.statement: Uses non-luminosity to dissolve philosophical scepticism (if evidence were luminous, evidence would be identical between ordinary and sceptical cases, but mental states are non-luminous so the argument fails) and explicitly rejects the phenomenal conception of evidence (a converging-to-the-empty-set sequence of ever-more-private appearances), translated as: KnowledgeOS's evidence must not be modeled as private/phenomenal appearances.

a_rows_sample.anchor: just as one cannot always know what one's evidence is, so one cannot always know what rationality requires of one. ... rationality is not luminous. ... the system cannot assume that Determination is always accessible.
a_rows_sample.statement: Extends non-luminosity specifically to rationality (one cannot always know what rationality requires), translated as: KnowledgeOS cannot assume Determination is always accessible/transparent to the system itself.

a_rows_sample.anchor: What to Adopt: Knowledge First ✅ ... Evidence = Knowledge ✅ ... Factive Mental States ✅ ... Non-Luminosity ✅ ... Margin for Error ✅ ... Anti-KK ✅ ... Knowledge Rule for Assertion ✅ ... What to Reject: Knowledge = Justified True Belief ❌ ... Phenomenal Evidence ❌ ... Transparency of Rationality ❌ ... Luminosity of Mental States ❌ ... Recommendation: Integrate ... into KnowledgeOS Theory v1.2
a_rows_sample.statement: Final recommendation table adopts all seven listed concepts (Knowledge First, Evidence=Knowledge, Factive Mental States, Non-Luminosity, Margin for Error, Anti-KK, Knowledge Rule for Assertion) unconditionally (all checked, no [PROP]/[OPEN] hedging) and recommends integrating them directly into KnowledgeOS Theory v1.2 -- a materially stronger, less-hedged recommendation than the same-day review (S2528), which instead treats most of these as PROP-status research candidates and explicitly places 'Evidence=Knowledge' on its own rejection list.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Cases in which p is known can be separated from cases in which p is false by a buffer of true-but-unknown cases. ... Known(p)\Rightarrow Margin(p,\Gamma)>0 ... the required margin can vary from point to point and need not be uniform ... Margin \neq Confidence ... Epistemic quality \neq scalar score
b_rows_sample.statement: Margin-for-error candidate: Known(p) => Margin(p,Gamma)>0 (not adopted as a universal law yet), motivating a margin/buffer relation between False, True-Unknown and Known rather than another flat categorical value; explicitly rejects deriving a scalar confidence or KnowledgeLevel in [0,1] from this, since the margin is proposition/environment-dependent and non-uniform.

a_rows_sample.anchor: a person may have insufficient evidence to establish a proposition, yet still need to act as if one hypothesis were true for practical or theoretical purposes. ... Claim: 'Hypothesis A is true' / Epistemic status: NOT_PROVEN / Decision: 'Proceed using A temporarily.' There is no contradiction.
a_rows_sample.statement: Cook Wilson's epistemic-vs-practical-decision distinction, worked as an example: acting on a NOT_PROVEN hypothesis is not contradictory, strengthening the justification for keeping a Decision Boundary strictly outside the Knowledge Core (NOT_PROVEN does not imply DO_NOT_ACT; VALIDATED does not imply MUST_ACT).

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS preserves the governed relationships among questions, beliefs, claims, evidence, inquiry, assessment, epistemic standing, authority, revision and action without collapsing epistemic status into practical decision or representation.
a_rows_sample.statement: Sharpens the previous KnowledgeOS definition to explicitly include questions/beliefs/inquiry/action and the non-collapse of epistemic status into practical decision or representation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Higher stakes demand greater assurance for rational action. ... Epistemic status != decision threshold. Outside Kernel: Risk policy, Decision threshold, Safety policy, Regulatory assurance, Business impact. ... Moral considerations ... should influence decision/governance policies, not redefine the meaning of epistemic truth.
a_rows_sample.statement: Pragmatic encroachment (higher stakes demand more evidence) and moral encroachment are both explicitly kept outside the Kernel as decision/governance policy rather than redefinitions of epistemic truth: Epistemic status != decision threshold.

b_rows_sample.anchor: inference — estimate the posterior distribution ... decision — use that posterior together with a loss function to choose an action. ... Evidence -> Inference -> Assessment -> Decision, and never collapse them.
b_rows_sample.statement: Called 'the single most important extraction': Bishop's inference-vs-decision-theory separation directly reinforces KnowledgeOS's existing Evidence->Inference->Assessment->Decision chain and strengthens the Godel invariant into a computational form: posterior != decision.

b_rows_sample.anchor: a reject option: when posterior probabilities are insufficiently decisive, the system should refuse to make the classification and hand the difficult case to a human expert. ... Decision = argmin_a E[L(a,theta)|evidence] where one possible action is a = REJECT.
b_rows_sample.statement: Bishop's reject option formalizes the platform's independently-derived 'escalate when uncertain' mechanism into a principled decision-theoretic form, giving KnowledgeOS a first-class ABSTAIN/ESCALATE/ACCEPT_WITH_UNCERTAINTY/INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE vocabulary instead of forcing TRUE/FALSE or STATE_A/STATE_B.

b_rows_sample.anchor: ExpectedTotalCost(model) = ComputeCost(model) + ExpectedDecisionLoss(model). ... choose m* = argmin_m ExpectedTotalCost(m) subject to assurance constraints. ... the inference ladder should therefore be risk-aware.
b_rows_sample.statement: Refines the prior Compute+ExpectedError routing formula into ExpectedTotalCost = ComputeCost + ExpectedDecisionLoss, incorporating Bishop's asymmetric false-positive/false-negative cost example, so the inference ladder path can vary by problem risk (a low-risk problem stops at a deterministic rule; a high-risk one may jump directly to an expensive method).

b_rows_sample.anchor: mixture of experts, where different experts model different regions of the input space and the gate determines which expert controls the prediction. ... BoundedContext ~= InferenceExpertBoundary.
b_rows_sample.statement: Mixture-of-experts (p(t|x)=sum_k pi_k(x)p(t|x,k)) mapped onto DDD: an 'epistemic experts' architecture where a Context Gate (a function of Context/Domain/EvidenceType/TemporalStructure/Risk, not merely an ML classifier) routes to a Temporal Expert (HSMM), Semantic Expert (SNF), or Governance Expert (Rules/DDD) -- BoundedContext approximately equals InferenceExpertBoundary.

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'inference-decision-separation-principle' POSSIBLY relates to 'epistemic-vs-practical-decision-separation' (batch B0012). Note: Bishop's inference-vs-decision-theory separation (posterior estimation vs loss-driven action choice) reframed as eight architectural principles: P1 Inference!=Decision; P2 Reject is a valid outcome (formalized as Decision=argmin_a E[L(a,theta)|evidence] with a=REJECT as an available action, giving KnowledgeOS a first-class ABSTAIN/ESCALATE/ACCEPT_WITH_UNCERTAINTY/INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE vocabulary instead of forced TRUE/FALSE); P3 structure before sophistication; P4 complexity must earn its cost via model evidence; P5 approximation must be observable (bound+convergence+validation); P6 model uncertainty is first-class and distinct from state uncertainty; P7 preserve posterior distributions until decision time rather than premature point estimates; P8 use heterogeneous experts (mixture-of-experts) where domains differ, aligning BoundedContext ~= InferenceExpertBoundary.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The Kernel owns everything necessary to protect the aggregate invariant during admission, and nothing more... the criterion's own key term ('the aggregate invariant', singular) is not specified
a_rows_sample.statement: S1-F009's 'equilibrium criterion' for Kernel membership contains a free variable: law carries eleven invariants (INV-KOS-IDENTITY-001 through HISTORY), and the criterion's output is entirely determined by which is substituted -- ranging from a near-minimal rule-evaluator to 'everything in' (the god-object F007 warns against). The criterion is therefore a schema, not a decision procedure, and its apparent power to reconcile the small-Kernel/large-Kernel dispute (S1-F007 vs S1-F008) is an artifact of underspecification, not resolution: 'compatibility with two opposed positions is not resolution of them; it is silence wearing a decision's clothing.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: The Kernel is a domain boundary, not a component... Then, in the same finding: 'Its implementation may be in the aggregate' and 'the Kernel is the part of the aggregate...'
a_rows_sample.statement: S1-F009 asserts the Kernel is 'a domain boundary, not a component' but then elaborates in component language ('the part of the aggregate...'), an unflagged type error: a set of rules is not a part of an aggregate, it is a constraint the aggregate satisfies. This means related findings (S1-F011's 'not a thing', S1-F012's 'domain space') may agree with F009's assertion while disagreeing with its elaboration, so any convergence claim must specify which half it converges on.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The equilibrium criterion itself... Verdict -> PRESERVE AS KNOWLEDGE ONLY, and per .1 only once its invariant is bound.
a_rows_sample.statement: Implementation verdicts for S1-F009: identity uniqueness/immutability -- DO NOT IMPLEMENT (already protected by INV-KOS-IDENTITY-001); admission event-completeness -- NEEDS FURTHER EVIDENCE (open question, not adjudicated); the equilibrium criterion itself -- PRESERVE AS KNOWLEDGE ONLY, useful as a review prompt but not implementable in any form until its invariant is bound; no new Kernel membership is supported by this artifact.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A member-list is a proposal about what the Kernel contains, and S2-F024.1 shows the corpus has no bound criterion for deciding such lists.
a_rows_sample.statement: Kernel-test verdict: DO NOT IMPLEMENT -- a member-list is a proposal, not a capability; implementing from a member list would repeat the exact failure S1-F007 diagnoses (membership by capability enumeration with no invariant named).
